explanations.explanation: Submit it is, friend. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities…” It's right at the top of his list, so he isn't whispering it. Nobody gets to skip the first item.

Keeping your distance sounds smart, like parking in the back row so nobody can find you. But Paul doesn't say hide. He says to “…submit to rulers and authorities…” The same verse adds being obedient and ready for good work, and you can't do either from the back row.

Questioning every order is the guy who reads the whole contract at the drive-thru window. Paul's word is different: “…submit to rulers and authorities…” Then he adds that believers should be “…obedient and ready for every good work.” That's a lot of readiness for somebody who wants a debate first.

I get why that sounds right, because we all love a good deed when it fits the schedule. But Paul never says that. He says the believers are to be “…ready for every good work…” Every one, convenient or not.
False is right, friend. Paul says the believers are to be “…obedient and ready for every good work…” He never gives a convenience clause. No fine print, no small print, nothing.
No one. That's the whole answer, and it's a big one. Paul says believers are “…to malign no one…” He doesn't leave a list of people who've earned it, and I checked twice.
Picking out the dishonest feels fair, doesn't it? Like giving yourself one tiny exception. But Paul writes “…to malign no one…” He doesn't carve out a category, so there's no exception to hide in.
The arrogant do make it tempting, I'll admit that. But Paul doesn't hand out exceptions. The text says believers are “…to malign no one…” That means the arrogant are covered too.
That's it, baker. Paul says to be “…peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.” Two soft words, and they're aimed at everyone. Not just the people who are easy to be nice to.

Bold and fearless sounds like a movie trailer, and I like it. But it isn't what Paul lists. He says to be “…peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.” That's a quieter kind of strong.

Strict and watchful sounds like a hall monitor with a clipboard. Paul's words are softer. He wants believers to be “…peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.” Put the clipboard down, friend.

explanations.answer: All sorts of desires and pleasures
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says we were “…enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures…” Notice the word "we." He's including himself in that group, and I think that's why it lands so gently.

explanations.answer: The rulers of our own land
explanations.explanation: I see why rulers came to mind, since they were in the first verse. But Paul told the believers to submit to rulers, not that they were enslaved to them. The thing that held us was “…all sorts of desires and pleasures…” That's a master you carry around inside.
Traditions of the elders aren't mentioned in this part of the letter. Paul says we were “…enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures…” It's what we wanted, not what we inherited.
That's the turn. “But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared…” After a list that heavy, the "but" lets you breathe. What appeared was kindness and love.
After that last list, I understand expecting anger. But Paul says what appeared was “…the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind…” The "but" turns the whole thing toward kindness.

A new set of laws would be a fast way to turn the page. But that isn't what Paul says. He says “…the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared…” What showed up was kindness and love.
I understand the pull. Good deeds feel like they should count for a lot. But Paul says it the other way: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done…” So our deeds aren't the reason.
False is right, friend. Paul writes, “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done…” So we didn't earn it, and nobody has to pretend they did.
Mercy. Paul says, “…but according to His mercy…” Mercy is getting what you couldn't earn, and I've been on the receiving end of that.
Law is a natural guess, since people love a rulebook. But Paul says God saved us “…according to His mercy…” The word he uses is mercy, not law.
Timing is a fine word, and bakers know it matters. But it isn't Paul's word here. He says God saved us “…according to His mercy…” Mercy is what that salvation rests on.
That's right. Paul says God saved us through “…the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.” It's the Spirit doing the renewing, and nobody has to do it themselves.
Church elders are worth respecting, but they aren't Paul's answer here. He says the renewal is “…by the Holy Spirit.” That's who does it.
Temple priests don't show up anywhere in this passage. Paul says it's “…renewal by the Holy Spirit.” The Spirit is the one who renews.
True. Paul says, “This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior…” Poured out, abundantly, through Jesus. I can't make that sentence any bigger than it already is.

It does sound like a lot to take in, but it's true. Paul says, “This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior…” The Spirit came through Jesus, and it was poured out abundantly.
Eternal life. Paul says we would become “…heirs with the hope of eternal life.” And he says we're justified by God's grace, so it's a gift, not a paycheck.
A promised land is a good guess for an heir, but it isn't what Paul says. He says we would become “…heirs with the hope of eternal life.” The hope is eternal life.
The word "heir" does sound like the reading of a will with a lot of zeros. But Paul doesn't say wealth. He says “…heirs with the hope of eternal life.” That hope is worth more than zeros anyway.
Good deeds, baker. Paul says he wants this stressed “…so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds.” Belief and doing good go together here.

Long debates are the opposite of what comes next. A moment later Paul says to avoid “…foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law…” What he wants believers to devote themselves to is “…good deeds.”
Fasting isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. Paul says those who have believed God should “…devote themselves to good deeds.” That's the thing he wants emphasized.
True. Paul says to avoid those things “…because these things are pointless and worthless.” He doesn't soften it, so neither will I.

I can see wanting to give a good argument some credit. But Paul says to avoid “…foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless.” So the statement is true.
Two. Paul says to “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition…” That's a warning, then another warning, and then the decision. It isn't a one-strike thing.
One warning is close, but it's short by a step. Paul says “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition…” That's two warnings before the rejecting.
Seven would be a very patient warning schedule, and I love the energy. But Paul says “…after a first and second admonition…” So it's two.
True. Paul says a divisive man is “…corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.” This is a heavier line in the letter, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.
It's a heavy line, so I understand wanting to say no. But Paul does say it: “…such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.” So the statement is true.

No trial shows up anywhere in this passage. Paul says, “…make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there.” He decided to spend the winter there, and that's the only reason he gives.
False is right. Paul says, “…make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there.” Winter plans, no courtroom.

Equip. Paul says, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.” It's about sending two men off with what they need, and I like a plan where nobody leaves empty-handed.

Test would make this a pop quiz for two travelers. Paul's word is different: “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.” The goal is that they have everything they need.

Correct sounds like Paul has a red pen out. But he says, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.” The word is equip, and the goal is that they have what they need.

explanations.answer: To meet the pressing needs of others
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, “…devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful.” The good works are for the people who have needs right now.

explanations.answer: To earn a place in God's family
explanations.explanation: That one is easy to slip into, but Paul already closed it off. He said God saved us “…not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy…” (Titus 3:5). The good works are “…to meet the pressing needs of others…”

explanations.answer: To win the respect of the rulers
explanations.explanation: Respect from the rulers isn't what Paul gives as the reason. He says the good works are “…to meet the pressing needs of others…” The reason is the people in need, not the audience.
